messages.content: Include keyword beneath in the 23-rd sentence, as the 34-th word of that sentence. Reference Text: Are there discrete random variables X, Y where the E(X) and E(Y) are finite but E(X + Y) is undefined or infinite?

message.content: The short answer to the reference question is no. A finite expectation means the random variable is integrable. Integrability requires both positive and negative parts to have finite sums. Therefore the absolute sum of value times probability is finite. If X is integrable, then its expectation is a well defined finite number. If Y is also integrable, then its expectation is likewise well defined. The sum of two integrable random variables is again integrable. This follows directly from the triangle inequality for expected absolute value. Specifically, the absolute expected value of the sum is bounded by the sum of absolute expected values. Hence the positive and negative parts of X plus Y are finite. Consequently, the expectation of X plus Y exists as a finite number. It cannot be undefined because cancellation of infinite parts is impossible under finite expectations. It cannot be infinite because integrability prevents any part from diverging. A common source of confusion is a conditionally convergent series. Such a series may depend on ordering if it is not absolutely convergent. The expectation of a random variable, however, is not a rearrangement game. It is defined through positive and negative parts before any cancellation. If both original expectations are finite, those parts are already controlled. Discrete examples do not change this rule, because the same definition applies. One can choose arbitrary probability distributions on a countable set. The integrability condition still forces the combined distribution to behave properly. Thus no discrete pair X and Y can satisfy the stated impossible requirement. The careful conclusion, after checking definitions, is that no such counterexample exists, because finite expectations guarantee integrability and a finite sum expectation, and the final point in this short answer is simply placed beneath it.
